"Substantially" means to a large, meaningful, real degree — not in a small or trivial way, but in a way that genuinely matters.

The feeling behind the word is solidity and weight. When something happens "substantially," it's not a minor blip. It's real. It's significant. It carries real substance.

Sense 1: To a great degree (= a lot, significantly)

This is the most common use. Something changed, grew, fell, or differed — and the degree was large and meaningful.

"The new laptop is substantially faster than the old one."

→ The speed difference is big. Not "a tiny bit faster" — meaningfully, noticeably faster.

"Prices have risen substantially over the past year."

→ Not a small uptick. A real, significant rise.

"Her health has improved substantially."

→ She's much better. The improvement is real and significant.

Where "substantially" sits on a scale:

  • slightly / a little → small degree
  • somewhat / moderately → medium degree
  • substantially / significantly / considerably → large degree ← this is where "substantially" lives
  • completely / entirely / totally → full degree

So "substantially" always implies more than minor, but not necessarily 100%.

Sense 2: In all the important/essential ways (= mostly, in substance)

Sometimes "substantially" doesn't just mean "a lot" — it means something is correct or true in all the core parts that matter, even if small edges differ.

"The two contracts are substantially the same."

→ The contracts are the same in every key part — rights, obligations, terms. Maybe the wording is slightly different in one clause, but the substance is identical.

"What she told the court was substantially true."

→ Her account was true in its important facts. Perhaps a minor detail was off, but the core of what she said was correct.

"The construction is substantially complete."

→ All the major work is done. Only minor finishing touches remain.

This second sense is especially common in legal, business, and formal writing. When a lawyer says a contract has been "substantially performed," they mean all the main obligations were fulfilled — perhaps not to 100% perfection, but in every material way.

There's no fixed number, but the word always communicates enough to matter — not trivially small.

A rough sense:

  • A "substantial" salary increase is probably 20–40%+, not 2%.
  • Two documents that are "substantially similar" probably overlap in 80–90%+ of their important content, not 15%.
  • A project that is "substantially complete" might be 85–95% done, not 50%.

The exact number is not the point. The point is: the degree is real, solid, and significant — not trivial, not negligible.

"Substantially" sounds formal. You'll encounter it most in:

  • Legal documents: "substantially similar," "substantially compliant," "substantially performed"
  • Business reports: "profits grew substantially," "costs were substantially reduced"
  • Academic writing: "the results differed substantially," "the evidence substantially supports"
  • News and journalism: "the bill was substantially amended"

In everyday casual conversation, people tend to say "a lot," "much," "mostly," or "pretty much" instead. But using "substantially" in speech doesn't sound strange — it just sounds precise and educated.

"Substantially" naturally pairs with these kinds of words:

Verbs of change: increase, decrease, grow, rise, fall, drop, improve, change, reduce
→ "Revenue has grown substantially."

Comparison words: different, similar, higher, lower, better, worse
→ "The second edition is substantially better."

Completion words: complete, finished, done
→ "The project is substantially complete."

Identity words: the same, similar, identical
→ "The two drafts are substantially the same."
How it compares to similar words

Significantly — The closest synonym. Almost always interchangeable with "substantially." The subtle difference: "significantly" often stresses importance (this matters, take note), while "substantially" often stresses size or solidity (this is big, real, and weighty). In most sentences, you can swap one for the other with no real loss of meaning.

Considerably — Also very close. Slightly more casual than "substantially." Often used when explicitly comparing two things: "The second version is considerably better." It emphasizes degree of comparison.

Largely / mostly — These mean "for the most part" or "in great proportion." They overlap with the second use of "substantially." "The report is largely accurate" ≈ "The report is substantially accurate." The difference: "largely/mostly" focuses on proportion (most of it), while "substantially" carries the extra idea of solidity and genuine weight.

Essentially / fundamentally — These go deeper. They mean something is true at its very core or nature. "They are essentially the same" = same at the deepest level. "They are substantially the same" = same in all the important parts. "Substantially" is a bit softer — it focuses on main parts, not the absolute foundation.

Greatly — Pure degree. "She improved greatly." Similar to "substantially," but "greatly" is simpler and more emotional. "Substantially" sounds more analytical and carries the extra flavor of weight and solidity.
One important word to not confuse it with

Substantially vs. Substantively — these look almost identical but mean different things.

  • Substantially = to a great degree; in all the important ways

"The two proposals are substantially similar." (They resemble each other to a large degree.)

  • Substantively = in terms of actual content or substance, as opposed to form, procedure, or surface appearance

"The committee made no substantive changes to the bill." (They didn't change the actual content — perhaps only formatting or wording.)

The confusion is easy to make, so keep this distinction in mind.

The word "substantially" is built around one idea: real, solid, meaningful weight. When you use it, you're telling your reader or listener: this is not trivial, this is not small, this is not on the edges — this is real and it matters.

It signals:

  • A large degree of something (prices rose substantially)
  • Genuine, solid completion or truth (substantially complete; substantially true)
  • Meaningful difference or sameness (substantially different; substantially the same)

Whenever you read or hear it, ask: "What is the speaker claiming is large, real, or important here?" The word is always answering that question — it's the signal that says "this deserves to be taken seriously."
